To outpace something or someone means to move, grow, or progress at a faster rate than them — and to keep doing so over time.

Think of the word in two parts:

  • Pace = the speed or rate at which something moves or happens
  • Out- = doing something more than, or better than, the other person/thing

Put them together: to outpace = to maintain a faster pace than someone or something else.

Imagine two runners on a track. Runner A starts covering ground faster than Runner B and keeps pulling ahead. Runner A is outpacing Runner B.

Notice: it's not just that A is ahead at one moment — it's that A is continuing to move faster, which means the gap between them keeps growing.

This is the heart of the word: not just being ahead, but consistently moving at a greater speed, so the distance between the two keeps widening.
The Bigger Picture (Figurative Use — Where the Word Really Lives)

In everyday writing and speech, "outpace" is almost never about actual running. It's used to describe anything that grows, increases, or progresses faster than something else. The "pace" can be the pace of growth, change, production, demand, technology — anything measurable over time.

Some examples:

  • Demand outpaces supply → People want products faster than companies can make them. The gap keeps growing.
  • Prices outpace wages → Prices rise faster than people's salaries. Over time, people can afford less and less.
  • Technology outpaces regulation → New technology develops faster than governments can make rules to control it.
  • A startup outpaces its rivals → The startup grows and expands faster than its competitors.
  • A student's curiosity outpaces the curriculum → The student wants to learn faster and deeper than the syllabus allows.

In every case, the same idea is at work: one thing is advancing at a greater rate than the other, and that difference is continuous and increasing.

When you use "outpace," you are saying three things at once:

  1. There is a comparison — two things are being measured against each other.
  2. One is faster/greater in rate — not just larger, but growing or moving more rapidly.
  3. This is an ongoing trend — not a one-time moment, but a sustained pattern.

This is why "outpace" is especially powerful in contexts like economics, business, science, and social trends — wherever rates of change matter.

You might wonder: why not just say "faster"?

The word "faster" describes a single moment. "Outpacing" describes a process that continues over time. When something outpaces something else, it means the gap is not static — it is actively widening as time goes on.

For example:

  • "The car is going faster than the bicycle" — a snapshot.
  • "Electric vehicles are outpacing petrol vehicles in sales" — a trend that has been building and continues to build.

This temporal, ongoing quality is what makes "outpace" distinct and precise.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are often used similarly, but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Outrun — more physical, more about literal speed; "he outran the dog."
  • Surpass — about exceeding a level, standard, or achievement; "she surpassed all expectations." (Does not strongly imply rate or speed.)
  • Outstrip — nearly identical to outpace; very common in formal writing. "Outstrip" can refer to degree as well as speed, e.g., "his talent outstripped his peers." Both are widely interchangeable.
  • Exceed — simply go beyond a limit or amount; "costs exceeded the budget." No sense of ongoing rate.

Outpace is the best word when you specifically want to talk about the speed or rate of change of one thing compared to another, especially in a sustained, ongoing way.

"Outpace" sits at a slightly formal register — you'll see it often in:

  • Journalism ("Renewable energy is outpacing fossil fuels in new installations.")
  • Business ("The company's revenue outpaced analyst expectations.")
  • Academic and scientific writing ("Population growth is outpacing food production in the region.")

That said, it is not stiff or difficult — it is widely understood and used across all levels of writing.

The word almost always follows this structure:

[Subject] outpaces [object]

  • Inflation outpaced economic growth.
  • Her ambition outpaced her resources.
  • AI development is outpacing our ability to understand it.

You can also write it in the past ("outpaced"), present continuous ("is outpacing"), or other tenses as needed.
A Simple Test: When to Use "Outpace"

Ask yourself: Is one thing advancing or growing at a faster rate than another, and is this a continuing trend?

If yes → outpace is your word.
One Sentence to Anchor It All

To outpace something means to consistently move, grow, or progress faster than it — so that the gap between the two keeps increasing over time.

Everything else about this word is just this idea applied to different contexts.
